title: Follow-up: VPC upgrade caused control-plane split due to lockfile race and DNS propagation lag
creator: Ravi Kapoor
description: Summary: During a staged Private/VPC control-plane minor version upgrade (2025.02.1 -> 2025.02.2) a race in the upgrade lock allocation caused two coordinator processes to believe they owned the same node set. Combined with a misconfigured DNS TTL and an out-of-order DNS update propagation, a subset of customer control-planes lost connectivity to the active leader and entered a transient split-brain. Impact: 9 customers experienced 3–12 minutes of control-plane API errors and failed health checks, causing autoscaling and management operations to stall. This ticket captures the post-incident analysis, mitigations already applied, and the concrete action items to prevent recurrence.
timeline: 2025-02-15T02:10Z - Automated canary upgrade started for region-eu-1 (batch size 10 clusters)
2025-02-15T02:27Z - Orchestrator observed lock acquisition failure on node coordinator A and retried; concurrent coordinator B acquired lock for overlapping node set
2025-02-15T02:29Z - Coordinator B completed restart of 6/10 control-plane replicas; coordinator A also attempted restarts, causing partial restart window
2025-02-15T02:31Z - DNS provider received update for control-plane IPs but TTL remained at 300s due to an upstream template bug; some client subnets continued to resolve old IPs
2025-02-15T02:34Z - Heartbeat flapping began as subsets of replicas reported conflicting leader identities; reconciliation loop evicted stale members leading to API errors
2025-02-15T02:45Z - On-call reverted the in-progress batch and applied emergency DNS TTL override to 60s; connectivity recovered for most clusters by 02:52Z
2025-02-15T03:05Z - Post-incident mitigation: roll restart to a single coordinator and manual verification of DNS propagation for the remaining batches
root_cause: Race condition in upgrade lock allocator: when two orchestrator workers attempted upgrades for adjacent node groups, lock ownership was not strictly single-writer — caused overlapping restarts
DNS template bug: automated DNS update script did not set the intended short TTL during IP swap, leaving 300s TTL in place
Lack of read-after-write verification for DNS changes: orchestrator assumed DNS updates were effective once API returned success
Insufficient canary controls: canary batch size and health-check thresholds did not detect partial leader disruption quickly
mitigations_taken: Immediate rollback of the in-progress batch to stable version 2025.02.1
Manual override of DNS TTL to 60s for affected zones and forced zone publish
Temporarily switched orchestrator to single-writer mode for all control-plane upgrades
Notified impacted customers and opened support tickets; applied one-time remediation to affected clusters
action_items: ENG-12590-A1: Add strict single-writer lock semantics to the upgrade allocator; owner=Marta Lopez; estimate=5; due=2025-02-22; status=In Progress
ENG-12590-A2: Implement read-after-write DNS verification step (query from multiple public resolvers before marking update succeeded); owner=Kenji Tanaka; estimate=3; due=2025-02-25; status=Planned
ENG-12590-A3: Reduce default DNS TTL template for control-plane IP swaps to 60s and add a safety check in CI; owner=Priya Singh; estimate=2; due=2025-02-21; status=In Progress
ENG-12590-A4: Introduce a control-plane canary policy: require leader-stability window of 120s before proceeding to next batch; owner=Ravi Kapoor; estimate=3; due=2025-02-26; status=Planned
ENG-12590-A5: Build an orchestration playbook and `redwoodctl` command for emergency TTL override and coordinated rollbacks; owner=Marta Lopez; estimate=2; due=2025-03-03; status=Planned
ENG-12590-A6: Run a chaos test that simulates staggered restarts + DNS delay to validate the new safeguards; owner=Reliability Team; estimate=5; due=2025-03-10; status=Planned
followup_notes: We should treat DNS as a first-class, eventual-consistency-dependent part of the upgrade path. Any operation that changes control-plane endpoint IPs must include verification and an automated rollback path if verification fails.

The orchestrator's lock model assumed disjoint node partitions; that assumption is unsafe during topology changes. Design review scheduled for 2025-02-18 to evaluate quorum-based coordination instead of coarse locks.
Customer communication: offer credit to affected customers and schedule post-mortem readout with mid-market customers in EU timezones (action owned by Support + Sales engineering).
Operational runbook additions: add explicit health-check checks for leader stability and DNS resolution from representative public resolvers before marking batch success.
